co_stein_boulder.blurb: The largest single stone in the wooded Redstone Boulders cluster, set in the trees just outside the village of Redstone, south of Carbondale at roughly 7,200 feet. It holds twenty problems and nothing else, which makes it a one-boulder destination for a session. The grades start with a couple of easy warm-ups, then jump to a dense middle of mid-range problems, with a handful of genuinely hard lines at the top end for strong boulderers. A short uphill walk on a trail from the parking pullout brings you to it, passing a smaller boulder on the way.

co_ridge_2_aka_satan_s_slab.blurb: The biggest of the four ridges in Skunk Canyon, in the Flatirons just north of Boulder. Most of the twenty routes here are traditionally protected, with a few sport lines and one boulder problem. The sunward face is a long, smooth slab with thin, sparsely protected climbing that feels harder than the typical Flatirons slab, while the opposite side overhangs and carries the sport routes. Grades run from easy fifth class up to the low 5.14 range, so there is something for confident moderate leaders and for experts. This is an adventurous, quiet canyon: bring a rack, expect multi-pitch outings and a long walk in.

ct_rattlesnake_cliff_climbs.blurb: A wooded traprock cliff at the south end of the Rattlesnake Mountain ridge in the Farmington area. The twenty-nine lines are mostly trad, with a few that are commonly top-roped. Grades range from beginner-level fourth and low fifth class up to a handful of 5.11 leads, but the bulk sit around 5.7 to 5.8, so it suits climbers building up their lead skills. The wall faces south and catches afternoon sun, which makes it a popular winter choice; in summer expect bugs and some seepage on the right side. Reach it on foot along the blue-blazed ridge trail.
ct_rattlesnake_cliff_climbs.parking_note: Leave the car along Route 6 and pick up the blue-blazed ridge trail heading south; the cliff is the last wall you reach on that trail.

ct_will_warren_s_den.blurb: A concentration of traprock boulders and blocks on top of Rattlesnake Mountain in Farmington, between the Green Wall and Rattlesnake Cliff. All twenty-seven problems are bouldering, split among a cave, a lower set of walls, a corridor and a small warm-up zone. Expect a mix of crimpy, slopey and steep, powerful moves, with grades from very easy up to the mid-V range plus a couple of harder ones, so beginners and strong boulderers both find something. Loose holds are a real possibility on this rock. Getting here takes a hike along the ridge trail, so pack light.
ct_will_warren_s_den.parking_note: Use the large roadside pull-off on Route 6 and follow the blue-blazed ridge trail south.
ct_will_warren_s_den.approach: Follow the blue-blazed ridge trail south from the Route 6 pull-off, passing the Porcupine and Green walls before you reach the boulders.

ct_old_quarry_walls.blurb: A small urban crag on the south end of West Rock Ridge above New Haven, built from the faces of an abandoned quarry. Most of the twenty-six routes are bolted sport lines, with a few trad and top-rope options. Grades start around 5.4 and stretch to the low 5.13 range, but the weight of the climbing is in the 5.9 to 5.12 bracket, so it is best for intermediate and strong leaders. The walls are short, and the rock is loose in places, so a helmet is a must and fixed gear deserves a careful look. The far-left wall sees the least sun and has the soundest stone.

ct_right_knee.blurb: One of the better climbing zones inside Sleeping Giant State Park in Hamden, a mix of boulder problems and short trad lines on traprock. The stone varies from soft and sandy to very hard, so test your holds. Boulder problems run from easy up to the upper V range, with several mid-grade lines, and the trad leads mostly stay in the easier fifth-class range, up to about 5.9, with a few top-rope options. Features include a cave and some overhanging faces. It makes a good stop for a casual, low-key session, reached by a short walk on the park trails from the lot.
